To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we determined the backbone and sidechain assignments of human profilin II.
we have assigned the backbone and side chain 1H, N and 13C resonances for human profilin IIA.
The human profilin II is an actin binding protein, which binds polyproline ligands and is involved in the regulation of cell motility.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new methods for the analysis of protein structures and dynamics by solid-state NMR.
the structural basis of the interaction between profilins and poly-l-proline-rich ligands.
the structural and functional characterization of profilins, a family of small, ubiquitous actin-binding proteins that regulate actin dynamics and function.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the backbone and sidechain 13C, 1H and 15N chemical shift assignments for profilin IIa are reported.
the assignment is correct and that the quality of the data is very good.
the backbone resonance assignment of the profilin IIa is complete and the sidechain assignment is nearly complete.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we were successful in obtaining a complete set of resonance assignments for human profilin II, and that we were able to identify the backbone amides of 12 residues that have been previously assigned as invisible by other methods.
the resonance assignment of the profilin IIa has been determined and that these data are available to the community through BMRB.
we were able to assign the backbone and sidechain 15N, 13C and 1H atoms of the human profilins Ia, IIa and IIb, and the backbone and side chain 15N and aliphatic 1H atoms for the human profilin Ia.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we have shown how a combination of 3D and 4D NMR experiments can be used to obtain backbone and sidechain resonance assignments for large proteins, in a time efficient manner.
the 1H chemical shift of the backbone amides is very sensitive to the presence of a bound ligand, even if the binding site is remote.
the 13C and 15N chemical shifts of the backbone and sidechain nuclei of the protein can be used to identify the binding sites of ligands.
